title.narrative: Output 8.1. Increased capacity of Member States to develop new or reformed sustainable national social protection strategies, policies or legal frameworks to extend coverage and enhance benefit adequacy

description.narrative: In June 2022, the Government of the Republic of Zambia approved the implementation of the Cash Plus Approach in its social protection programming, aiming to enhance the comprehensiveness of social protection coverage enjoyed by nearly 1 million current social cash transfer (SCT) beneficiaries. The approach, as articulated in the form of a Cabinet Memorandum providing policy guidance across all government ministries, is based upon a concept note and roadmap for the Cash Plus approach, which outline targeted linkages between SCT and complimentary social protection services, including the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS). Implementation of the approach is coordinated by the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services whose role has been established to address inter-generational transmission of poverty, the multi-dimensionality of poverty and the need to combine a social protection floor (which is provided by the SCT) with a social protection ladder (which would be other programmes, such as empowerment programmes that help beneficiaries find sustainable income generation so that they can get out of poverty and eventually exit the SCT). A fully institutionalised Cash Plus Approach shifts service provision from trying to provide a minimum to everybody towards providing a comprehensive response to the multiple needs of a particular household. The ILO, through the UN-Joint Programme and the IRISH AID project played a very critical role in supporting a microsimulation research exercise through a tax-benefit analysis model called the Micro-ZAMOD. The research was spearheaded by the Zambia Institute for Policy Analysis and Research (ZIPAR) with technical support from UNU-WIDER, Southern African Social Protection Experts Network (SASPEN), SASPRI, and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). Other stakeholders involved included the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services and other line Ministries selected across the Human and Social Development Cluster of the 8th National Development Plan. The findings of the research were launched through a Policy Brief which fed into the policy recommendations for the Cash Plus Policy Approach, which was eventually approved by Cabinet.

description.narrative: In March 2022, the National AIDS Council (NAC) operationalized a gender-responsive capacity building programme on enterprise development targeted at people living with HIV, young women and young female sex workers in the informal economy and by September 2022 and June 2023 respectively, 120 beneficiaries had been trained. Through socio-economic empowerment, the intervention aims to contribute towards improved livelihoods as a means of reducing vulnerability to HIV. The interventions were informed by a UNAIDS report of 2020 which showed that, in 2020, six in seven adolescents aged between 15—19 years old acquiring HIV in Southern Africa were girls and that more than 23000 young women died from AIDS-related illnesses in 2020 , and that keeping girls in secondary school and providing them with life skills, training and employment opportunities is key to ending the AIDS pandemic in Africa. The interventions were also informed by a Joint government and UN GBVII Baseline and Socio-Economic Impact Assessment of COVID-19 whose one of the findings showed that women suffer multiple vulnerabilities, including socio economic related. With funding from UNAIDS, In September 2022 and June 2023, the ILO in collaboration with the National AIDS Council (NAC), the Zambian Network of People Living with HIV (NZP+), the Key Population Consortium and Pride Community Health Organisation, with funding from UNAIDS Country Envelop, conducted capacity enhancement in Gender and Entrepreneurship Together (GET Ahead) for Women in Enterprise and GET Ahead for Youth in Enterprise for thirty (30) People Living with HIV (19 females and 11 males), and , 90 Young Women including Young Female Sex Workers from the informal involved in trading of food and non food commodities such as clothes and hair products.
